Salesforce just told the world it built its own brain for CRM. Then, in the same week, it kept selling you access to everyone else's brains too. Watch that carefully, because it tells you exactly what Salesforce thinks its own data is worth, and what it thinks the rest of the model market is worth.

Here's the setup. Salesforce trained a new model called Koa. It didn't build the base from scratch. It took Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Super, an open model, meaning (Nvidia's own words) one "released with publicly accessible weights, data, or training recipes that developers can inspect, customize, and deploy on their own infrastructure." Salesforce then post-trained it on synthetic data and kept the whole thing running inside its own walls. No customer records went anywhere near it, or so they say.

Think of it like ordering a pizza base from a wholesaler, then doing your own toppings in your own kitchen, and refusing to let anyone else taste it until you've already told the papers it's the best pizza in town. That's the shape of this. So let's check what's actually in the box, and what's just the smell of good marketing.

Ask yourself, before we go further: if you ran a CRM company sitting on decades of customer workflow data, would you rent a brain from Anthropic or OpenAI, or would you build your own on someone else's base and keep it locked in your own kitchen? Salesforce just answered that question for itself. Twice. Differently. On the same day.

**The base, Nemotron 3 Super: REAL.** Salesforce's own technical paper puts numbers next to this. On its CRM Bench, the Nemotron-3-Super-120B base model scored 0.84. Koa, the version Salesforce post-trained on top of it, scored 0.86. That's a real, measured lift, and it's a small one. Salesforce didn't invent a new brain. It sanded down a borrowed one. Nothing wrong with that. Just don't call it from-scratch invention, because the paper itself doesn't.

**"27 years of Salesforce CRM intelligence": THEATRE.** This is the line built to make you picture millions of real customer records feeding the model. It didn't happen. Salesforce's own release says: "No customer data was used to train the Koa reasoning model. Its training corpus was built entirely from synthetic scenarios." And the technical paper explains how those scenarios got made: a "frozen helper model" played the customer in every training conversation, plus the tool responses, plus the judge marking the homework. So the 27 years is a flavour, not an ingredient. Salesforce studied what real customers do, then had one AI pretend to be the customer while another AI graded the result. That's a fair way to train a model. It is not 27 years of customer intelligence going into the dough.

**"Matches or exceeds leading model performance" with "three times fewer errors": THEATRE.** Here's where the pizza box says more than the pizza delivers. Salesforce's press release claims Koa "already matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions with three times fewer errors." But Salesforce's own paper has a table, and the table says something different. On CRM Bench, GPT-5.5 scored 0.90. Claude Opus 4.8 scored 0.87. Koa scored 0.86. That's not matching or exceeding the leading models. That's finishing third out of three, by the paper's own numbers, and the paper says as much itself: Koa "surpasses a strong proprietary baseline (GPT-4.1) while remaining below the strongest frontier models." We went looking for the "three times fewer errors" figure inside the technical paper. We could not find it there. It may exist somewhere Salesforce hasn't shown, but it isn't in the document doing the measuring. TechTimes checked too, and reported that no independent auditor has published a verification of the results, because the benchmark grading the pizza is the same kitchen that baked it.

**Kept in-house: REAL.** This part checks out completely. Because Nemotron is open, meaning Salesforce could download the weights and run everything on its own machines, Salesforce controls the whole loop. Rohan Kumar, Salesforce's president of platform and engineering, said at Dreamforce: "Not a single byte of customer data was used." Salesforce hosts Koa, trains Koa, and serves Koa entirely inside its own trust boundary. That's the actual, structural point of choosing an open base over a closed one: you get to own the kitchen. Right now Koa is running for select pilot customers, including Formula 1, UChicago Medicine, and Xero. General availability is expected winter 2026, in the US only.

So here's the fork, in plain terms. The pizza base is genuinely open and genuinely reheated well, that's real. The claim that it beats the best pizza in town is theatre dressed as a scoreboard. And the decision to bake it at home, in a kitchen nobody else can inspect, is completely real, and arguably the actual news. Salesforce isn't proving Koa is smarter than Claude or GPT-5.5. It's proving it doesn't need to be, as long as it's cheap enough, private enough, and good enough at CRM chores that customers stop asking who baked it.

Guess, clearly labelled: the reason Salesforce built its own benchmark and graded its own homework isn't secrecy for its own sake. It's that an independent benchmark would show the gap to GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 that Salesforce's own paper already shows, just with less marketing spin around it.

## OUR PREDICTION

By 30 September 2027, at least one of SAP, Oracle or Workday will launch an AI model of its own, built by post-training another company's open-weight model, echoing exactly the Nemotron-into-Koa move.

How sure we are: 78%.
